CST201.start: Trace a loop on paper, then reuse it to process an array. Once the indices make sense, move the same work into a function and revisit it using pointers.

1.title: Read a short C expression
1.focus: Start with types, formatted input and output, and operator precedence. Keep a tiny example for each operator family.
1.try: Predict the results of integer and floating-point division with the same operands, then run both expressions and explain the difference.

questions.focus: Explain operator precedence and associativity with an example.
Review header files and show how C bitwise operators work.

2.title: Trace the branch and the loop
2.focus: Compare if–else with switch. For each loop type (for, while and do–while), note when the condition is checked and what changes each iteration.
2.try: Trace a digit-sum loop with input 402. Include a separate test for zero and check what happens before the first iteration.

questions.focus: Compare entry-controlled and exit-controlled loops; practise the accompanying loop program.
Illustrate switch–case, then write a program to sum a series of running totals.

3.title: Work through arrays and strings
3.focus: Write the valid index range before touching an array. For strings, identify the terminator and the buffer size before using a library function.
3.try: Sketch a 3 × 3 matrix, mark its diagonal indices, and write a loop that adds only those elements. Then draw how a short string is stored.

questions.focus: Define a C string and demonstrate four standard string-handling functions.
Read an integer matrix and compute its diagonal sum.

4.title: Turn a solution into a function
4.focus: Match the prototype, call and return type. Compare variable scope and lifetime, then practise spotting a recursion base case.
4.try: Write a factorial function and trace the stack by hand for input 3. Test the base case separately.

questions.focus: Explain C storage classes using small declarations as examples.
Generate Fibonacci terms with recursion, then write a loop version.

5.title: Draw pointers before writing code
5.focus: Label each variable, address and pointed-to value. Then revise pointer-based array traversal and the allocation/free lifecycle.
5.try: Draw a small dynamically allocated array. Write the allocation, failure check, traversal and cleanup in that order.

questions.focus: Explain when to use malloc, calloc, realloc and free.
Sum array elements through a pointer and explain the related memory operations.

checklist: Trace one loop on a normal input and a boundary case.
Explain the index bounds of a matrix and the terminator of a C string.
Identify the return value and base case of a recursive function.
Draw what a pointer refers to and say where allocated memory is freed.

CST203.topics: Python basics, functions, files and Django
CST203.start: Start by predicting the output of short snippets. Then pass a collection to a function, process text from a file, and finish by drawing how a Django page is served.

1.title: Choose a type and predict the result
1.focus: Compare lists, tuples and dictionaries. Predict slicing, indexing, string operations and the output of simple expressions.
1.try: Make a list of five values. Predict two slices and try changing an element; explain how the same operation differs on a tuple.

questions.focus: Show how split and join work, and explain why Python strings are immutable.
Compare lists, tuples and dictionaries; illustrate indexing and slicing.

2.title: Dry-run conditions and loops
2.focus: Read indentation before tracing code. Compare for and while, then test what changes when a loop meets break, continue, pass or else.
2.try: Write a loop that adds only the odd values in a list. Dry-run it on a mixed list and on an empty list.

questions.focus: Explain the different Python loops with examples.
Illustrate break, continue and pass, then practise a prime-number check.

3.title: Package small, testable functions
3.focus: Practise arguments and scope before modules and packages. Check which names belong to the function and what its caller gets back.
3.try: Write a function with one default argument, call it with and without that argument, and move it to a module that you import.

questions.focus: Demonstrate positional, default and variable-length function arguments.
Compare a module with a package and distinguish the four kinds of variable scope asked for in the paper.

4.title: Read a file and extract a match
4.focus: Choose the correct file mode before using a read or write method. Then predict which pieces of a string the regular-expression call returns.
4.try: Read a short text file, count its lines, and use a regular expression to pick out digit groups from the text.

questions.focus: Explain file access modes and give examples of read and write.
Practise the regular-expression subparts on match locations and match, split and findall.

5.title: Follow a Django request
5.focus: Map a URL to a view and a template. Then revisit forms, validation, template inheritance and static files in the notes.
5.try: Draw the route for a page that lists books, labelling what receives the URL and what displays the list. Add where a form would be validated.

questions.focus: Explain how a Django template refers to a static file.
Explain Django’s architecture and how it relates to MVC, focusing on the framework subpart.

checklist: Predict a slice and the output of a loop before you run either.
Show a call with a default argument and explain what the function returns.
Pick a file mode and a regular-expression method for a small task.
Sketch a Django URL, view and template flow without looking at the notes.

CST205.topics: Stacks, queues, linked lists, trees and graphs
CST205.start: If you know the basic terms, start with stack and queue traces, then draw linked lists. If the terminology feels unfamiliar, review Unit 1 before that sequence.

1.title: Name the structure and its operations
1.focus: Organise examples by how elements are arranged. Connect each example to real operations such as insertion, deletion and traversal.
1.try: Pick a linear structure and a non-linear one. Sketch both and describe what it means to visit every element in each.

questions.focus: Classify primitive, non-primitive, linear and non-linear structures, and compare data types with data structures.
Explain common operations on data structures and compare linear with non-linear structures.

2.title: Trace stacks and circular queues
2.focus: Record top, front and rear after each operation. Revisit postfix evaluation and write a recursion trace with a clear base case.
2.try: Evaluate a short postfix expression with a stack. Then trace a circular queue until rear wraps, showing its full and empty states.

questions.focus: Write push and pop, then evaluate the given postfix expression using a stack.
Write pseudocode for an array-backed circular queue.
Compare recursion with iteration and write the recursive Tower of Hanoi routine.

3.title: Draw before and after each list operation
3.focus: Handle the head, tail and an interior node separately. In a doubly linked list, check the links in both directions.
3.try: On paper, insert into an empty list, insert in the middle, and delete the last node. Label which references change each time.

questions.focus: Write singly linked-list algorithms for insertion after a given node and for counting nodes.
Compare arrays and linked lists, then explain when a doubly linked list helps.

4.title: Separate tree and graph traces
4.focus: Write tree traversals next to the diagram and identify where an AVL rotation is needed. For graphs, label the starting vertex and visited set.
4.try: Take a small tree and write all three traversal orders. On a small graph, run BFS and DFS from the same vertex and compare the orders.

questions.focus: Reconstruct a binary tree from the given in-order and pre-order traversals.
Explain AVL rotations and apply them to the insertion sequence in the paper.
Compare depth-first and breadth-first search in the graph-traversal subpart.

checklist: Check empty and full conditions in a stack or queue trace.
Draw a linked-list insertion and label the updated links.
Redo a tree traversal and an AVL rotation without notes.
State the starting vertex and neighbour order when tracing a graph.

CST207.start: Start with the computer block diagram and 8086 registers. Trace one short assembly sequence while the registers are fresh, then give memory and computer arithmetic their own study sessions.

1.title: Draw the path that data takes
1.focus: Label the processor, memory, I/O and buses. Use a before-and-after register diagram for transfers and shift micro-operations.
1.try: Draw the Von Neumann block diagram without notes. Use a small register example to trace a logical shift in each direction.

questions.focus: Define a logical shift; practise illustrating it with a register example.
Draw and label the Von Neumann structure and explain the computer bus architecture.

2.title: Trace arithmetic, control and the pipeline
2.focus: Keep separate diagrams for the control unit and instruction pipeline. For a multiplication or division algorithm, track every register update.
2.try: Trace a small signed multiplication using the taught register format. Draw a separate pipeline timeline and mark where a dependency can delay an instruction.

questions.focus: Explain restoring division and trace the given signed multiplication with Booth’s algorithm.
Explain pipelining and distinguish different kinds of pipeline hazards.
Describe the instruction cycle and draw the control-memory block diagram asked for in the paper.

3.title: Label the 8086 before memorising instructions
3.focus: Identify the BIU, EU and the main registers. For an instruction, distinguish the addressing mode from the instruction’s operation.
3.try: Draw the BIU and EU and label several registers. Explain which part of each example instruction tells you where its operand comes from.

questions.focus: Define an addressing mode and illustrate different 8086 modes with examples.
Explain what the 8086 BIU and EU do and compare its minimum and maximum modes.

4.title: Track the state after each instruction
4.focus: Start with moves and arithmetic, then trace a branch or call using the values you have written down. Revisit directives, procedures and macros after the instruction trace.
4.try: Write a short sequence that adds two register values and stores the result elsewhere. Trace what each instruction changes before adding a branch.

questions.focus: Interpret what a MOV instruction does to the destination register in the paper’s objective item.
Choose the assembly steps that add two register values and keep the result in the requested register.

5.title: Keep cache, virtual memory and interfacing separate
5.focus: Draw where an address goes in each case: to a cache location, through address translation, or to a selected memory device.
5.try: Sketch a direct-mapped cache lookup, then draw a separate RAM/ROM address-selection example from the notes.

questions.focus: Describe how RAM and ROM/EPROM are interfaced to the 8086.
Explain direct-mapped cache and define virtual memory.

checklist: Draw the computer blocks and explain what moves along each bus.
Label the 8086 BIU and EU, and identify an instruction’s addressing mode.
Show the intermediate register values in an arithmetic or assembly trace.
Explain a pipeline hazard, a cache lookup and address translation as three separate ideas.

CST209.start: Start with a short complexity trace. Reuse the same small inputs to compare sorts and searches, then put graph algorithms on paper and label each intermediate choice.

1.title: Count work before naming the growth rate
1.focus: Identify the input size, the operation being counted and the case you are analysing. Compare divide and conquer, greedy and dynamic programming using examples.
1.try: Count iterations for a loop that increments by one and one that doubles its index. Show your reasoning for both before writing the asymptotic bound.

questions.focus: Explain the characteristics of an algorithm and distinguish the asymptotic notations asked for.
Illustrate divide and conquer and compare it with dynamic programming.

2.title: Show the intermediate sorting passes
2.focus: Practise a simple in-place sort, a divide-and-conquer sort and a linear-time sort from the syllabus. Distinguish time cost from extra space.
2.try: Trace selection sort and merge sort on the same short list with a duplicate value. Write the array after each pass or merge.

questions.focus: Trace selection sort and explain its worst-case time complexity.
Compare merge, quick and heap sorts, then trace radix sort on the values given.

3.title: State the search assumptions
3.focus: State whether the input is sorted. For trees, trace the search path, and for hashing, show where a collision lands and how it is resolved.
3.try: Find a present key and an absent key with binary search. Then place two keys in a small hash table so you can demonstrate one collision.

questions.focus: Write and explain recursive binary search.
Define hashing and describe ways to resolve collisions.
Show insertion and deletion in a binary search tree and explain why balance matters.

4.title: Choose the graph algorithm for the goal
4.focus: Keep shortest paths, minimum spanning trees and topological order distinct. Check the graph type and edge assumptions before choosing an algorithm.
4.try: Run Prim’s and Dijkstra’s algorithms on the same small undirected graph with positive weights. Record each chosen edge or updated distance and explain the different goals.

questions.focus: Explain Prim’s algorithm and construct a minimum spanning tree with Kruskal’s algorithm using the given graph.
Write Bellman–Ford and trace it on the graph supplied with the question.
Explain Dijkstra’s single-source shortest-path algorithm and write a short note on topological sorting.

checklist: Name the input size and case before writing a time bound.
Show passes for a sort, and test a binary search with an absent key.
Trace a BST update or a hash collision without notes.
Name the graph goal and edge assumptions before starting the trace.
